chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, all together from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Khadir al-Nakha'i, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who has a debt due from another man, and the debtor denies it: He (peace be upon him) said: 'If the creditor asks him to swear an oath, it is not for him (the creditor) to take anything (if he swears); and if he leaves it and does not ask him to swear, then he (the creditor) is upon his right (to claim the debt).'

key_terms.اسْتَحْلَفَهُ: He asked him to swear an oath
key_terms.فَلَيْسَ لَهُ أَنْ يَأْخُذَ شَيْئاً: It is not for him to take anything

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on debt collection if the debtor denies the debt and refuses to swear an oath?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi establishes the legal principle of 'al-yamin wa al-shahada' (oath and testimony) in Shia jurisprudence, highlighting the creditor's strategic choice between securing a definitive settlement via the debtor's oath or preserving the claim for further evidentiary proof. It reflects the Imami emphasis on procedural fairness, where the creditor's decision to forgo the oath is viewed as a voluntary retention of their right rather than a waiver of the debt itself. This mechanism underscores the importance of the oath as a conclusive legal instrument in the absence of written documentation.
